98	// ── Wave builder (Kahn's algorithm) ──────────────────────────────────────────
99	
100	function buildWaves(lanePlan) {
101	  const lanes = lanePlan.lanes
102	  const ids = Object.keys(lanes)
103	  const inDeg = {}
104	  const adj = {}
105	
106	  for (const id of ids) {
107	    const deps = lanes[id].depends_on || []
108	    for (const dep of deps) {
109	      if (!lanes[dep]) throw new Error(`Task '${id}' depends on '${dep}', which does not exist in the lane plan`)
110	    }
111	    inDeg[id] = deps.length
112	    for (const dep of deps) {
113	      ;(adj[dep] = adj[dep] || []).push(id)
114	    }
115	  }
116	
117	  const waves = []
118	  let queue = ids.filter(id => inDeg[id] === 0).sort()
119	
120	  while (queue.length > 0) {
121	    waves.push([...queue])
122	    const next = []
123	    for (const id of queue) {
124	      for (const child of adj[id] || []) {
125	        inDeg[child]--
126	        if (inDeg[child] === 0) next.push(child)
127	      }
128	    }
129	    queue = next.sort()
130	  }
131	
132	  const placed = new Set(waves.flat())
133	  const cyclic = ids.filter(id => !placed.has(id))
134	  if (cyclic.length > 0) throw new Error(`Cyclic dependency detected among tasks: ${cyclic.sort().join(', ')}`)
135	
136	  return waves
137	}

139	// ── File classification ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────

141	function classifyFiles(files) {
142	  const isTest = f => {
143	    const base = f.split('/').pop()
144	    return base.startsWith('test_') || base.endsWith('_test.py') ||
145	      base.endsWith('.test.ts') || base.endsWith('.test.js') ||
146	      base.endsWith('.spec.ts') || base.endsWith('.spec.js') ||
147	      base.endsWith('_test.go') || base.endsWith('Tests.swift') ||
148	      f.includes('/tests/') || f.includes('/Tests/') ||
149	      base === 'conftest.py'
150	  }
151	  const testFiles = (files || []).filter(isTest)
152	  const implFiles = (files || []).filter(f => !isTest(f))
153	  return { testFiles, implFiles }
154	}

156	// ── Text-to-JSON parser for datum-cli agents ───────────────────────────────
157	
158	function parseAgentJson(text, fallback) {
159	  if (!text || typeof text !== 'string') return fallback || null
160	  const cleaned = text.replace(/```[a-z]*\n?/g, '').trim()
161	  const start = cleaned.search(/[{[]/)
162	  const end = Math.max(cleaned.lastIndexOf('}'), cleaned.lastIndexOf(']'))
163	  if (start === -1 || end === -1) return fallback || null
164	  try { return JSON.parse(cleaned.slice(start, end + 1)) }
165	  catch { return fallback || null }
166	}

168	// ── Lane context shell command builder ─────────────────────────────────────

170	function laneCtxCmd(packet, wt) {
171	  const ctx = JSON.stringify({
172	    task_id: packet.task_id,
173	    stage: packet.stage,
174	    allowed_write_files: packet.allowed_write_files,
175	    forbidden_write_files: packet.forbidden_write_files,
176	    commit_prefix: packet.commit_prefix,

180	}
181	
182	// ── JSON packet builder ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
183	
184	function buildPacket(taskId, testFiles, implFiles, lane, wt, cfg, stage, extras) {
185	  return {
186	    schema_version: '1.0',
187	    task_id: taskId,
188	    stage,
189	    title: lane.title,
190	    working_directory: wt,
191	    test_command: cfg.testCommand,
192	    acceptance_criteria: lane.acceptance_criteria || [],
193	    red_note: lane.red_note || '',
194	    allowed_write_files: stage === 'RED' ? testFiles
195	      : stage === 'GREEN' ? implFiles
196	      : [...testFiles, ...implFiles],
197	    forbidden_write_files: stage === 'RED' ? implFiles
198	      : stage === 'GREEN' ? testFiles
199	      : [],
200	    commit_prefix: stage === 'RED' ? `red(${taskId})`
201	      : stage === 'GREEN' ? `green(${taskId})`
202	      : `refactor(${taskId})`,
203	    ...extras,
204	  }
205	}

207	// ── Per-lane TDD saga ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

209	async function runLane(taskId, lanePlan, worktreePaths, cfg) {
210	  const lane = lanePlan.lanes[taskId]
211	  const wt = worktreePaths[taskId]
212	  const isStructural = lane.stage === 'structural'
213	
214	  // #5: compute once per lane
215	  const { testFiles, implFiles } = classifyFiles(lane.files)
216	  const acStr = (lane.acceptance_criteria || []).join('\n')
217	
218	  // Per-lane test command: only run THIS lane's test files, not the global set
219	  const laneTestCmd = testFiles.length > 0
220	    ? `uv run pytest ${testFiles.join(' ')} -x -q`
221	    : cfg.testCommand

225

228	    if (!r) return { task_id: taskId, status: 'failed', stage: 'REFACTOR', error: 'refactor failed' }
229	    return { task_id: taskId, status: 'completed' }

232	  // ── Skeleton preflight (E2: capture output directly, no separate read agent) ──
233	  const skeletonText = await agent(

235	    `--tasks ${cfg.lanePlanPath} --output .datum/runs/${cfg.runId}/preflight-${taskId}.json 2>&1`,

501	    log(`[${taskId}] REFACTOR: skipped (${(preCheck && preCheck.reason) || 'nothing to improve'})`)

505	  log(`[${taskId}] REFACTOR: proceeding (${preCheck.reason})`)
506

509	
510	  const refactor = await agent(
511	    `SETUP (run first): ${refactorCtxCmd}\n` +

514	  )

516	  if (!refactor) {

518	    return null
519	  }
520	  if (!refactor.committed && refactor.failure_reason && !refactor.failure_reason.toLowerCase().includes('nothing to')) {
521	    log(`[${taskId}] REFACTOR FAILED: ${refactor.failure_reason}`)

526	    return { verified: true }
527	  }
528	
529	  const checkText = await agent(
530	    `cd "${wt}" && datum verify-stage green --repo "${wt}" --test-command "${laneCfg.testCommand}"\nReturn ONLY the JSON output, nothing else.`,
531	    { label: `verify-refactor:${taskId}`, phase: 'Act', model: 'haiku' }
532	  )
533	  const check = parseAgentJson(checkText, { verified: false })
534	
535	  if (!check || !check.verified) {

544	const a = (typeof args === 'string') ? JSON.parse(args) : (args || {})

572	}

574	// ── Auto-partition: group waves into batches of ≤5 tasks ────────────────
575	
576	const MAX_BATCH = 5
577	
578	// Split oversized waves — intra-wave tasks are independent, so splitting is safe
579	const splitWaves = []
580	for (const wave of waves) {
581	  if (wave.length <= MAX_BATCH) {
582	    splitWaves.push(wave)

595	    batches.push(curBatch)

597	    curCount = 0

602	if (curBatch.length > 0) batches.push(curBatch)

612

631	    { label: `root-wt${batchTag}`, phase: 'Setup', model: 'haiku' }
632	  )

640	    { label: `setup-wt${batchTag}`, phase: 'Setup', model: 'haiku' }
641	  )

643

648	  // Write once to root, then cp to lanes (avoids N× JSON inline in shell command)

message.content: does local git have task ids? like TASK-0001 is it a built in feature?

content.text:
No, Git has no built-in task/ticket ID system. Commit messages, branches, and tags are freestrings — any `TASK-0001` pattern you see is a convention enforced by the team or tooling (Jira prefixes, Linear IDs, etc.), not something Git tracks or validates natively.

The closest built-in concepts are:
- **Commit SHA** — the actual unique identifier Git uses
- **`git notes`** — lets you attach metadata to commits after the fact, but nobody uses it for task tracking

If you want enforced task IDs on commits, that's a `commit-msg` hook or a tool like datum's `commit_prefix` in the lane context. Want me to wire something up?

content.text:
Yes. GitHub sub-issues are just regular issues with a parent link. Every sub-issue gets its own `#number` — `#201`, `#202`, etc. There's no separate ID system; they're first-class issues that happen to have a parent.

So the wireframe is accurate — `#201` is both the sub-issue ID and the lane ID. Commits would literally say `red(#201)`, `green(#201)`.

The Claude Code workflow runtime is a sandboxed evaluator. Workflow scripts **cannot use `import` or `require()`**. They run as self-contained JS with globals (`agent()`, `parallel()`, `phase()`, `log()`, `args`) injected. This is by design for deterministic journaling and resume support.

This means the decomposition must happen **within the single file** using code organization, or via `workflow()` calls to separate named workflows. True multi-file module extraction is not possible.

---

## 2. What Is Extractable (Pure Logic)

These functions are pure -- data in, data out, no side effects, no `agent()` / `log()` calls:

| Function | Lines | Tier | Line Count | Unit-Testable Today? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `buildWaves(lanePlan)` | L100-L137 | Logic | 38 | Yes -- Kahn's algorithm, throws on cycles |
| `classifyFiles(files)` | L141-L154 | Logic | 14 | Yes -- regex matching, no I/O |
| `parseAgentJson(text, fallback)` | L158-L166 | Logic | 9 | Yes -- string parsing |
| `laneCtxCmd(packet, wt)` | L170-L180 | Logic | 11 | Yes -- builds a shell string |
| `buildPacket(taskId, ...)` | L184-L205 | Logic | 22 | Yes -- object construction |
| Contract extraction (inline in `runLane`) | L339-L352 | Logic | 14 | Yes if extracted -- regex + filter |

Total pure logic: ~108 lines. These could be in a shared file if imports were supported, but they cannot be.

The 6 schemas (L31-L96) are pure data: **66 lines**.

---

## 3. What Has Mixed Tiers

`runLane()` (L209-L521, **313 lines**) is the biggest problem. It mixes:
- **Logic**: `classifyFiles()` call (L215), `contractSummary` extraction (L339-L352), skeptic cross-validation (L480-L484), file ownership check (L506-L511)
- **Data/Infra**: every `agent()` call (RED, GREEN, verify, reflect, skeptic, refactor), `parallel()` calls
- **Presentation**: 30+ `log()` calls for progress reporting

`runRefactor()` (L524-L580, **57 lines**) is similarly mixed but smaller.

The main body (L582-L899, **318 lines**) is mostly Data/Infra orchestration (Setup, Merge, Cleanup phases) with Presentation (logging).

---

## 4. Concrete Proposal

Given the no-import constraint, I propose **two strategies** in priority order:

### Strategy A: Inline Reorganization (works today, no runtime risk)

Reorganize the single file into clearly delimited sections with section headers. This doesn't hit DPS-103's 500-line cap, but it establishes the tier boundaries for when imports become available.

```
// ══ TIER: SCHEMAS (pure data) ══════════════════════════
// Lines 31-96: all 6 schemas

// ══ TIER: LOGIC (pure functions, zero side effects) ════
// buildWaves, classifyFiles, parseAgentJson, laneCtxCmd, buildPacket
// + extracted: extractContractSummary, crossValidateBugs, checkFileOwnership

// ══ TIER: ORCHESTRATION (agent calls, git ops) ═════════
// runLane, runRefactor

// ══ TIER: MAIN (phase flow, batch loop) ════════════════
// Topology, batch loop (Setup/Act/Merge/Cleanup), Docs, Triage
```

**Specific extractions from `runLane()`:**

1. **`extractContractSummary(acceptanceCriteria)`** -- pull L338-L352 into a standalone function. Currently inline. Pure logic, 15 lines, trivially testable.

2. **`crossValidateBugs(skepticResults, lenses)`** -- pull L469-L503 (the skeptic consensus logic) into a function. Returns `{ allBugs, brokenCount, crossValidated }`. Pure logic, 35 lines.

3. **`checkFileOwnership(testFiles, implFiles, stageResults)`** -- pull L506-L511 into a function returning violations array. Pure logic, 6 lines.

This brings the pure-logic section to ~160 lines and reduces `runLane()` from 313 to ~255 lines.

### Strategy B: Sub-Workflow Composition (larger split, more risk)

Split into two workflow files:

**File 1: `skills/datum-tdd-act.js`** (~480 lines) -- the orchestrator
- `meta` export
- All schemas
- All pure logic functions
- Main body: Topology, batch loop, Docs, Triage phases
- `runRefactor()` stays here (57 lines, not worth a separate workflow)

**File 2: `skills/datum-tdd-lane.js`** (~400 lines) -- the lane saga
- Its own `meta` export
- `runLane()` reimplemented as a standalone workflow accepting `{ taskId, lanePlan, worktreePath, cfg }` as `args`
- Invoked from the orchestrator as: `await workflow("datum-tdd-lane", { taskId, lanePlan, worktreePaths, cfg })`

This hits the 500-line cap for both files. But there are significant risks:
- **`workflow()` calls may not support returning structured results** the way `runLane()` currently returns `{ task_id, status, stage, error }`. Need to verify the `workflow()` return contract.
- **The DAG scheduler (L696-L728) uses `Promise` resolvers** for dependency gating across lanes. If each lane is a separate workflow, the DAG coordination mechanism needs rethinking -- you can't share `depPromises` closures across `workflow()` boundaries.
- **Resume semantics change**: a separate workflow has its own journaling scope, so partial resume behavior may differ.

---

## 5. Schema Placement

The 6 schemas total 66 lines. They should stay in the orchestrator file regardless of strategy. They're referenced by `{ schema: STAGE_RESULT_SCHEMA }` in `agent()` options -- if lane execution moves to a sub-workflow, that sub-workflow needs its own copy (since no imports). Duplication is the cost.

If the runtime ever supports imports, schemas move to `skills/datum-tdd-schemas.js`.

---

## 6. Prompt Templates

The agent prompts are currently inline strings in `runLane()`. Extracting them to named constants (e.g., `RED_PROMPT_TEMPLATE`, `GREEN_PROMPT_TEMPLATE`) is **worth doing**:

- **Pro**: makes `runLane()` shorter by ~60 lines, makes prompts auditable in one place, eases prompt iteration without hunting through control flow
- **Con**: templates need interpolation (working dir, packet JSON, etc.), so they'd need to be functions: `const redPrompt = (ctxCmd, packetStr) => \`...\``
- **Verdict**: Extract as template functions at the top of the file, right after schemas. Low risk, high readability gain.

---

## 7. Recommended Priority Order

1. **Extract `extractContractSummary()`** -- inline logic buried in `runLane()`, easy win, immediately testable. (15 min)

2. **Extract `crossValidateBugs()`** -- the skeptic consensus block is complex enough to deserve its own function with unit tests. (15 min)

3. **Extract prompt template functions** -- 5-6 template functions, reduces `runLane()` by ~60 lines. (30 min)

4. **Reorganize file with tier section headers** -- cosmetic but establishes the boundary for future splits. (10 min)

5. **Evaluate `workflow()` return contract** -- before attempting Strategy B, verify that `await workflow("name", args)` returns the workflow's `return` value. If it does, proceed to split. If it doesn't, Strategy B is blocked.

6. **Split `runLane` into sub-workflow** (Strategy B) -- only after step 5 confirms feasibility and after finding a DAG coordination pattern that works across workflow boundaries.

---

## 8. Migration Risk Summary

| Change | Risk | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Extract pure functions (within file) | Near zero | Same file, same scope, no runtime change |
| Extract prompt templates | Low | String interpolation refactor, testable |
| Tier section headers | Zero | Comments only |
| Sub-workflow split | **Medium-High** | DAG Promise coordination breaks, resume semantics change, return value contract unclear, schema duplication |

---

## 9. Minimum Split to Hit DPS-103 (500 Lines)

The file is 899 lines. To get under 500, you need to remove ~400 lines. The only viable cut is extracting `runLane()` (313 lines) + `runRefactor()` (57 lines) + the schemas they reference (66 lines if duplicated) into a sub-workflow. That gets the orchestrator to ~460 lines and the lane workflow to ~440 lines.

But this is blocked by the DAG coordination problem described above. The practical path is:

1. Do steps 1-4 from the priority list (gets the file more readable but still ~800 lines)
2. Accept the DPS-103 violation with an explicit waiver comment explaining the runtime constraint
3. Revisit when/if Claude Code adds `import` support to workflows

The 500-line cap exists to prevent tangled files. This file is long but not tangled -- each function has a clear boundary. The right response to DPS-103 here is a documented exception, not a forced split that breaks the DAG scheduler.</result>

# RTK - Rust Token Killer

**Usage**: Token-optimized CLI proxy (60-90% savings on dev operations)

## Meta Commands (always use rtk directly)

```bash
rtk gain              # Show token savings analytics
rtk gain --history    # Show command usage history with savings
rtk discover          # Analyze Claude Code history for missed opportunities
rtk proxy <cmd>       # Execute raw command without filtering (for debugging)
```

## Installation Verification

```bash
rtk --version         # Should show: rtk X.Y.Z
rtk gain              # Should work (not "command not found")
which rtk             # Verify correct binary
```

⚠️ **Name collision**: If `rtk gain` fails, you may have reachingforthejack/rtk (Rust Type Kit) installed instead.

## Hook-Based Usage

All other commands are automatically rewritten by the Claude Code hook.
Example: `git status` → `rtk git status` (transparent, 0 tokens overhead)

Refer to CLAUDE.md for full command reference.

# WFC Coding Steering (Distilled)

This document consolidates 12 fragmented Claude rule files into a single, token-efficient steering doctrine for LLM context injection. 

## Core Architecture (DPS)
- **DPS-100**: **Three-Tier Separation**. Presentation (I/O, formatting), Logic (pure business rules), Data (persistence). Presentation never touches Data directly.
- **DPS-101**: **Functional Core / Imperative Shell**. Business logic must be pure (data in, data out). All side effects (DB, HTTP) live at the edges.
- **DPS-102**: **Boundary Validation**. Validate external input shape (Pydantic/Zod) immediately at the boundary. No logic executes on unvalidated payloads.
- **DPS-103**: **File Size Cap**. Hard cap of 500 lines per file. Split via functional seams, not arbitrary line cuts.

## Resiliency & State
- **DPS-200**: **Timeouts & Retries**. Every external call (HTTP, DB, subprocess) must have an explicit timeout and capped backoff retry (e.g. `tenacity`).
- **DPS-201**: **Idempotency**. All mutating operations must be idempotent (upserts, idempotency keys, dedup before side-effects).
- **DPS-202**: **Explicit State**. Represent state via Enums/Literals. Transitions must be guarded and explicit.
- **DPS-203**: **Structured Errors**. Errors must never be silently swallowed. API errors must return `{ code, message, correlationId }`.
- **DPS-204**: **No Silent Fallbacks**. Never use `??` or `||` to mask data that shouldn't be missing. Throw and fail fast instead.

## Testing & TDD
- **TDD-001**: **Red-Green Mandatory**. Always write the failing test first (RED), confirm the failure, then write code (GREEN). Post-hoc testing is forbidden.
- **TDD-002**: **Strong Assertions**. Tests must verify specific business outcomes. If deleting the function body doesn't fail the test, the test is worthless.
- **TDD-003**: **No Fake Logic**. Do not hardcode return values just to make tests pass.
- **TDD-004**: **Negative Paths Required**. Always test invalid inputs, retry exhaustion, timeouts, and state violations.

## AI & Tooling Discipline
- **AI-001**: **Zero Bash Readers**. NEVER use `cat`, `head`, `tail`, or `less` in a Bash tool to read files. Use the native Read/View tool.
- **AI-002**: **No Invented APIs**. Do not call APIs, methods, or imports that you haven't confirmed exist in the codebase or official docs.
- **AI-003**: **Minimal Diffs**. Only change what is required for the task. No drive-by rewrites or unrequested refactors.
- **AI-004**: **Preserve Debug Logs**. Never remove diagnostic logs in the same commit as a bug fix.
- **AI-005**: **Memory Recall First**. Always query `wfc helpers recall "<task>"` before implementing to check for prior decisions/findings.

## Python Specifics
- **PY-001**: **Toolchain**. Python 3.12+, `uv`, `black`, `ruff`, `pytest`, `httpx`, `structlog`, `orjson`.
- **PY-002**: **Execution**. Never use bare `python` or `pytest`. Always use `uv run python` and `uv run pytest`.

## Safeguard & Security
- **SEC-001**: **No Dynamic Execution**. `eval()`, `os.system()`, `shell=True` are blocked via PreToolUse hooks.
- **SEC-002**: **Lockfiles Mandatory**. Never install packages without a lockfile. Reject dependencies published <90 days ago.

Here's what the TDD agents are still doing beyond their single core job:

**1. Test running / verification** — RED, GREEN, and REFACTOR agents all run `datum verify-stage` themselves (lines 414, 528, 658). Verification is a separate concern from writing code.

**2. Git resets on retry** — Lines 386, 485, 651 spawn ad-hoc haiku agents to run `git checkout -- . && git clean -fd`. That's git operation, same class as commits.

**3. Git revert on failed refactor** — Line 666 spawns haiku to `git revert --no-edit HEAD`. Another git operation outside `commitStage`.

**4. File reading for context** — The reflect agent (line 418) and refactor pre-check (line 607) read source files just to evaluate. That's a read concern, not a write concern — but it's reasonable for those agents.

**5. `datum skeleton` execution** — Line 349 runs a CLI tool. The skeleton agent is a shell executor, not a writer.

**6. Lane plan reading** — Line 692 spawns a haiku just to `Read` a JSON file. Workflow scripts can't read files natively, but this is still a "fetch data" job being done by an agent.

**7. Worktree setup/cleanup/merge** — Lines 738-863 spawn agents for `git worktree` and `datum worktrees` commands. These are infrastructure/git operations.

**8. Docs agent still commits directly** — Line 899 uses `STAGE_RESULT_SCHEMA` (with `committed`), meaning the docs agent handles its own git. Inconsistent with the single-writer pattern.

The biggest wins for single-function extraction:

| Current | Extract to | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `git checkout/clean` resets (3 places) | `resetWorktree()` git agent | Same class as `commitStage` — git ops, not code writing |
| `git revert` on bad refactor | `revertWorktree()` git agent | Git op |
| `datum verify-stage` (3 places) | `verifyStage()` dedicated function | Verification ≠ writing. Currently scattered, same pattern repeated 3x |
| Docs agent self-committing | Route through `commitStage()` | Consistency — single writer everywhere |

The four that would have the most impact: **resetWorktree**, **revertWorktree**, **verifyStage**, and **docs commit routing**. Want me to build them?

Right — workflow scripts are plain JavaScript, no TypeScript. The runtime evaluates them in an async sandbox with no `import`/`require`, no Node.js APIs, no type annotations. `: string[]` or `interface Foo` would be a parse error.

skills/

  datum-tdd-act-setup.js    ← Setup phase

  datum-tdd-act-docs.js     ← Docs phase
  datum-tdd-act-triage.js   ← Triage phase
```

Each child gets `args` passed from the parent — the lane plan, config, worktree paths, etc. They share the concurrency cap, agent counter, and token budget. The schemas and pure functions get duplicated into the files that need them (or we put shared stuff in a `datum-tdd-act-lib.js` that the orchestrator `workflow()`-calls first to validate, and each child re-declares what it needs).

The duplication is the tradeoff — no imports means each file carries its own copies of schemas and helpers. But the files stay under 500 lines each and each phase is independently testable.

215	function crossValidateBugs(skepticResults, lenses) {
216	  const allBugs = []
217	  let brokenCount = 0
218	  for (let i = 0; i < lenses.length; i++) {
219	    const s = skepticResults[i]
220	    if (!s) continue
221	    if (s.verdict === 'BROKEN') brokenCount++
222	    for (const bug of (s.bugs_found || [])) {
223	      allBugs.push({ ...bug, lens: lenses[i].key })
224	    }
225	  }
226	  const bugDescs = allBugs.map(b => b.description.toLowerCase().slice(0, 60))
227	  const crossValidated = allBugs.filter((bug, idx) => {
228	    const myDesc = bugDescs[idx]
229	    return bugDescs.filter((d, j) => j !== idx && d === myDesc).length > 0
230	  })
231	  return { allBugs, brokenCount, crossValidated }

content.text:
Pushed.

Yes — write in TypeScript, transpile to JS before execution. The workflow sandbox only cares about the final `.js` file, so as long as the build step strips types, it works. The compile step catches type errors before runtime.

Two approaches:

1. **`tsc --noEmit` for checking only** — keep writing `.ts` files alongside, run `tsc` as a gate, but manually maintain the `.js`. Lightweight but doesn't actually generate the JS.

2. **Full build step** — write `.ts` source files in `skills/src/`, transpile with `tsc` or `esbuild` to `skills/datum-tdd-act-*.js`. The `.js` files become build artifacts. A `scripts/build-workflows.sh` runs the transpile.

Option 2 is the real deal. `esbuild` is fast (sub-second), strips types without needing a full `tsc` config, and handles ESM output natively. You'd get:

```
skills/
  src/                          ← source of truth
    datum-tdd-act.ts
    datum-tdd-act-lane.ts
    datum-tdd-act-setup.ts
    shared/types.ts             ← interfaces, schema types
  datum-tdd-act.js              ← generated (gitignored? or committed?)
  datum-tdd-act-lane.js         ← generated
```

The catch: workflow scripts can't `import`, so the transpiler needs to **inline** shared types, not leave `import` statements. `esbuild --bundle` does this — it resolves imports and outputs a single self-contained file per entry point.

So: TypeScript source with shared interfaces → `esbuild --bundle` per entry point → self-contained `.js` files with zero imports. Type safety at dev time, plain JS at runtime. Want me to wire it up?

content.text:
Compile-time guarantees on things that currently blow up at runtime inside the workflow sandbox — where errors are expensive (each agent call costs tokens and wall-clock time):

**What you catch before a single agent runs:**

| Bug class | Today (JS) | With TS |
|---|---|---|
| Typo in schema field name | Agent returns `{ commited: true }`, passes silently | `Property 'commited' does not exist on type CommitResult` |
| Wrong args to child workflow | `a.batchRunid` → `undefined` → setup throws mid-run | `Property 'batchRunid' does not exist on type SetupArgs` |
| Missing required field in packet | `buildPacket` returns `{ stage: undefined }` → agent confused | `Argument of type '{}' is not assignable — missing 'stage'` |
| Wrong return type from function | `verifyStage` returns string but caller expects object | `Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'VerifyResult'` |
| Schema/function signature drift | You change `WRITE_RESULT_SCHEMA` but forget to update `runLane` | Interface mismatch caught at compile |
| Passing wrong array to `commitStage` | `commitStage(id, wt, prefix, testFiles, 'GREEN')` — should be `implFiles` | Typed overloads or branded types catch the swap |

**What it doesn't give you:**

- Runtime validation of agent output (agents can still return garbage JSON — schemas handle that)
- Correctness of prompts (that's a human/testing problem)
- Any performance improvement

The ROI question: you have 6 workflow files with ~30 function signatures crossing boundaries, and each bad call burns a haiku or sonnet invocation before you find out. One `tsc` run catches all of them for zero tokens.

Worth it if you're actively iterating on the pipeline. Not worth it if it's stable and you're just running it.

Perfect! Now I have all six files. Let me compile a comprehensive map of the boundaries.

## TypeScript Types Map for Datum TDD Workflow

### 1. SCHEMA Declarations

**Files using WRITE_RESULT_SCHEMA:**
- `datum-tdd-act-lane.js` (lines 11-19)
- `datum-tdd-act-docs.js` (lines 9-17)

**Files using COMMIT_RESULT_SCHEMA:**
- `datum-tdd-act-lane.js` (lines 21-31)
- `datum-tdd-act-docs.js` (lines 19-29)

**Unique schemas:**
- `REFLECT_SCHEMA` (datum-tdd-act-lane.js, lines 33-41)
- `SKEPTIC_SCHEMA` (datum-tdd-act-lane.js, lines 43-59)
- `REFACTOR_CHECK_SCHEMA` (datum-tdd-act-lane.js, lines 61-68 AND datum-tdd-act-docs.js, lines 31-38) — **duplicated**
- `TRIAGE_SCHEMA` (datum-tdd-act-triage.js, lines 9-26)

---

### 2. Async Function Declarations (Boundary Contracts)

#### **datum-tdd-act.js** (Orchestrator)
| Function | Parameters | Return Shape | Called From | Calls |
|----------|-----------|--------------|-------------|-------|
| `buildWaves` | `lanePlan: { lanes: {...}, topological_order: [...], total_lanes: number }` | `waves: string[][]` | main | (internal utility) |

**Main execution**: No formal function; uses `workflow()` calls.

#### **datum-tdd-act-setup.js**
| Function | Parameters | Return Shape |
|----------|-----------|--------------|
| `parseAgentJson` | `text: string, fallback?: any` | `any` |
| *implicit main* | `args: { batchRunId, epicBranch, batchLaneIds: string[], lanePlan, batchTag }` | `{ worktreePaths: {[taskId]: string} }` |

#### **datum-tdd-act-lane.js**
| Function | Parameters | Return Shape |
|----------|-----------|--------------|
| `classifyFiles` | `files: string[]` | `{ testFiles: string[], implFiles: string[] }` |
| `parseAgentJson` | `text: string, fallback?: any` | `any` |
| `laneCtxCmd` | `packet: {...}, wt: string` | `string` (shell command) |
| `extractContractSummary` | `acceptanceCriteria: string[]` | `{ function, args, returns, raises, ac }[]` |
| `crossValidateBugs` | `skepticResults: {...}[], lenses: {...}[]` | `{ allBugs, brokenCount, crossValidated }` |
| `buildPacket` | `taskId, testFiles, implFiles, lane, wt, cfg, stage, extras` | `{ schema_version, task_id, stage, title, working_directory, test_command, acceptance_criteria, ..., [extras] }` |
| `commitStage` | `taskId, wt, commitPrefix, allowedFiles, stage` | `{ committed: boolean, commit_sha?: string, files_staged?: string[], violations?: string[], failure_reason?: string }` |
| `resetWorktree` | `taskId, wt, stage` | `void` |
| `revertLastCommit` | `taskId, wt, stage` | `void` |
| `verifyStage` | `taskId, wt, stage, testCommand` | `{ verified: boolean, error?: string, test_signal?: {...}, ... }` |
| `runSkeleton` | `taskId, wt, cfg` | `{ impl_stubs?: string[], existing_api?: {...}, ... }` |
| `runLane` | `taskId, lanePlan, worktreePaths, cfg` | `{ task_id, status: 'completed'\|'failed', stage?: string, error?: string }` |
| `runRefactor` | `taskId, lane, testFiles, implFiles, wt, cfg` | `{ verified: boolean } \| null` |
| *implicit main* | `args: { batchLaneIds, lanePlan, worktreePaths: {[id]: string}, cfg, priorFailures, batchTag }` | `{ results: {[taskId]: LaneResult} }` |

#### **datum-tdd-act-merge.js**
| Function | Parameters | Return Shape |
|----------|-----------|--------------|
| *implicit main* | `args: { completedIds: string[], epicBranch, batchRunId, topoOrder: string[], batchTag }` | `{ merged: boolean }` |

#### **datum-tdd-act-docs.js**
| Function | Parameters | Return Shape |
|----------|-----------|--------------|
| `commitDocs` | `wt: string, commitPrefix: string, allowedFiles: string[]` | `{ committed: boolean, commit_sha?: string, files_staged?: string[], violations?: string[], failure_reason?: string }` |
| *implicit main* | `args: { completedLanes: string[], lanePlan, runId }` | `{ synced: boolean, files?: string[] }` |

#### **datum-tdd-act-triage.js**
| Function | Parameters | Return Shape |
|----------|-----------|--------------|
| *implicit main* | `args: { failures: string[], results: {[id]: {...}}, lanePlan, runId, epicBranch }` | `{ filed: number }` |

---

### 3. Args Destructuring (Parent → Child Contracts)

#### **Setup (datum-tdd-act-setup.js)**
```
{
  batchRunId: string,
  epicBranch: string,
  batchLaneIds: string[],
  lanePlan: { lanes: {...}, topological_order: string[], total_lanes: number },
  batchTag: string
}
```

#### **Act (datum-tdd-act-lane.js)**
```
{
  batchLaneIds: string[],
  lanePlan: { lanes: {...}, topological_order: string[], total_lanes: number },
  worktreePaths: { [taskId]: string },
  cfg: { lanePlanPath, epicBranch, runId, testCommand, language },
  priorFailures: string[],
  batchTag: string
}
```

#### **Merge (datum-tdd-act-merge.js)**
```
{
  epicBranch: string,
  completedIds: string[],
  batchRunId: string,
  topoOrder: string[],
  batchTag: string
}
```

#### **Docs (datum-tdd-act-docs.js)**
```
{
  completedLanes: string[],
  lanePlan: { lanes: {...}, topological_order: string[], total_lanes: number },
  runId: string
}
```

#### **Triage (datum-tdd-act-triage.js)**
```
{
  failures: string[],
  results: { [taskId]: { status, stage, error } },
  lanePlan: { lanes: {...}, topological_order: string[], total_lanes: number },
  runId: string,
  epicBranch: string
}
```

---

### 4. Return Statements (Child → Parent Contracts)

| Workflow | Returns |
|----------|---------|
| **Setup** | `{ worktreePaths: {[taskId: string]: string} }` |
| **Act** | `{ results: {[taskId: string]: { task_id, status: 'completed'\|'failed', stage?: string, error?: string }} }` |
| **Merge** | `{ merged: boolean }` |
| **Docs** | `{ synced: boolean, files?: string[] }` |
| **Triage** | `{ filed: number }` |

---

### 5. Pure Functions Duplicated Across Files

| Function | Files | Signature |
|----------|-------|-----------|
| **parseAgentJson** | `datum-tdd-act-setup.js`, `datum-tdd-act-lane.js` | `(text: string, fallback?: any) => any` |
| **REFACTOR_CHECK_SCHEMA** | `datum-tdd-act-lane.js`, `datum-tdd-act-docs.js` | Same structure: `{ should_refactor: boolean, reason?: string }` |
| **COMMIT_RESULT_SCHEMA** | `datum-tdd-act-lane.js`, `datum-tdd-act-docs.js` | Identical object schema |
| **WRITE_RESULT_SCHEMA** | `datum-tdd-act-lane.js`, `datum-tdd-act-docs.js` | Identical object schema |

---

### 6. Key Data Shapes (Lane Plan & Result Objects)

#### **LanePlan** (passed to all child workflows)
```
{
  lanes: {
    [taskId]: {
      title: string,
      files: string[],
      depends_on?: string[],
      acceptance_criteria?: string[],
      red_note?: string,
      stage?: 'structural' | 'behavioral',
      green_model?: string
    }
  },
  topological_order: string[],
  total_lanes: number
}
```

#### **Lane Result** (returned by runLane)
```
{
  task_id: string,
  status: 'completed' | 'failed',
  stage?: 'RED' | 'GREEN' | 'REFACTOR' | 'SKELETON' | 'SKIPPED' | 'CRASH' | 'UNKNOWN',
  error?: string
}
```

#### **Configuration (cfg)** (passed to each lane)
```
{
  lanePlanPath: string,
  epicBranch: string,
  runId: string,
  testCommand: string,
  language: string
}
```

#### **Task Packet** (buildPacket return)
```
{
  schema_version: '1.0',
  task_id: string,
  stage: 'RED' | 'GREEN' | 'REFACTOR',
  title: string,
  working_directory: string,
  test_command: string,
  acceptance_criteria: string[],
  red_note: string,
  allowed_write_files: string[],
  forbidden_write_files: string[],
  commit_prefix: string,
  [extras: string]: any
}
```

---

### 7. Agent Call Patterns (Schema Injections)

Each child workflow calls `agent()` with an injected schema:

- **WRITE_RESULT_SCHEMA** → RED, GREEN, REFACTOR, DOCS agents
- **COMMIT_RESULT_SCHEMA** → GIT agents (commitStage, commitDocs)
- **REFLECT_SCHEMA** → Test quality reflection agents
- **SKEPTIC_SCHEMA** → Adversarial review agents (3 lenses: edge, error, contract)
- **REFACTOR_CHECK_SCHEMA** → Refactor decision agents
- **TRIAGE_SCHEMA** → Issue categorization agents
- **VERIFY_SCHEMA** (implied) → Stage verification agents

---

## Recommendation for TypeScript Interfaces

Create a shared `types.ts` module with these root interfaces:

1. **WorkflowArgs interfaces** (one per child workflow)
2. **WorkflowResult interfaces** (one per child workflow)
3. **Schema interfaces** (reuse duplicated schemas as types)
4. **Domain objects**: `LanePlan`, `Lane`, `LaneResult`, `TaskPacket`, `AgentConfig`, `WorktreePaths`
5. **Agent result types**: `WriteResult`, `CommitResult`, `ReflectResult`, `SkepticResult`, `RefactorCheckResult`, `TriageResult`, `VerifyResult`

This will eliminate the 6-7 duplicated schema definitions and make the cross-workflow contracts explicit and type-safe.

You are researching optimal prompt engineering patterns for a multi-agent TDD pipeline. The pipeline has 6 distinct agent roles, each called via Claude's workflow `agent()` function with structured output schemas. Each agent runs in a git worktree and operates on Python code.

## The Agent Roles

Research best prompting practices for each of these roles. For each, I need:
- What the current prompt does (I'll give you the gist)
- What research/best practices say about prompting for this type of task
- Concrete recommendations for improving the prompt
- A recommended rewritten prompt

### 1. RED TDD Agent (model: sonnet)
**Current behavior**: Writes FAILING tests for acceptance criteria. Must append tests, never delete. Must avoid `raise NotImplementedError` (causes false green). Must call actual methods that don't exist yet so tests fail with AttributeError/AssertionError.
**Schema output**: `{ files_written: string[], success: boolean, failure_reason?: string }`
**Key failure modes**: Tests pass when they shouldn't (green blindness), tests are too weak (low quality score), agent writes implementation code instead of tests, agent runs git commands.

### 2. GREEN TDD Agent (model: sonnet, escalates to opus)
**Current behavior**: Writes MINIMUM implementation code to make failing tests pass. Gets a task packet with test_signal (error messages), contract_summary (function signatures), impl_stubs (skeleton code), existing_api (module shape).
**Schema output**: `{ files_written: string[], success: boolean, failure_reason?: string }`
**Key failure modes**: Over-engineering (writes more than needed), doesn't read test errors carefully, starts from scratch instead of filling in stubs, breaks existing tests.

### 3. REFACTOR Agent (model: sonnet)
**Current behavior**: Cleans up implementation without changing behavior. Gets task packet with allowed/forbidden write files.
**Schema output**: `{ files_written: string[], success: boolean, failure_reason?: string }`
**Key failure modes**: Changes behavior (breaks tests), refactors too aggressively, touches files outside its lane.

### 4. GIT COMMIT Agent (model: haiku, escalates to sonnet)
**Current behavior**: Single writer pattern. Validates file ownership (only allowed files), stages, commits with prefix. Never edits source files.
**Schema output**: `{ committed: boolean, commit_sha?: string, files_staged?: string[], violations?: string[], failure_reason?: string }`
**Key failure modes**: Commits files outside the allowed list, edits source files, fails on dirty index or detached HEAD.

### 5. TEST QUALITY Evaluator / Reflect (model: haiku)
**Current behavior**: Reads test files, scores 0-10 against acceptance criteria, reports gaps.
**Schema output**: `{ score: number, reasoning: string, gaps: string[] }`
**Key failure modes**: Inflated scores, vague reasoning, misses obvious gaps.

### 6. Adversarial Skeptic (model: haiku for edge/error, sonnet for contract)
**Current behavior**: Three lenses run in parallel — edge cases, error paths, behavioral contracts. Each returns verdict (PASS/FRAGILE/BROKEN) with bugs found.
**Schema output**: `{ bugs_found: [{description, evidence, severity}], confidence: number, verdict: 'PASS'|'FRAGILE'|'BROKEN' }`
**Key failure modes**: False positives (reports bugs that aren't real), too lenient (PASS on everything), vague bug descriptions without evidence.

### 7. CODE QUALITY Evaluator / Refactor Pre-check (model: haiku)
**Current behavior**: Reads files and decides whether refactoring is needed. Conservative — should say false if code is clean.
**Schema output**: `{ should_refactor: boolean, reason: string }`
**Key failure modes**: Always says true (wastes a sonnet call), vague reasons.

### 8. Docs Sync Agent (model: sonnet)
**Current behavior**: Updates existing docs that reference changed code. Adds doc sections for new public APIs. Never creates new doc files.
**Schema output**: `{ files_written: string[], success: boolean, failure_reason?: string }`
**Key failure modes**: Creates new doc files, uses "uv run" instead of "datum <cmd>", touches CHANGELOG.

## Research Areas

For each agent role, research and recommend:

1. **Role framing**: How to establish the agent's identity and constraints. Research shows that role-based prompting ("You are an X") has specific effects — what does the literature say about role prompts for code-generation vs evaluation tasks?

2. **Task decomposition**: Should the prompt give step-by-step instructions or high-level goals? What works better for coding agents?

3. **Negative constraints**: Current prompts use many "do NOT" rules. Research on negative vs positive framing in prompts — is there a better way?

4. **Evidence-first patterns**: For evaluator agents (reflect, skeptic), should we require evidence before verdict? What prompting patterns reduce hallucinated findings?

5. **Chain-of-thought vs direct**: Should coding agents reason step-by-step, or just produce output? Different for writing code vs evaluating code?

6. **Structured output alignment**: Best practices for prompting when the output must conform to a JSON schema.

7. **Context window efficiency**: These prompts include large JSON task packets. Best practices for presenting structured context to coding agents.

## Deliverable

For each of the 8 agent roles, provide:
1. Analysis of current prompt strengths/weaknesses (2-3 sentences)
2. Research-backed recommendations (bullet points)
3. A complete rewritten prompt template (ready to use, with ${variable} placeholders matching the current codebase)

Keep the rewritten prompts practical — they'll be used in production. Don't add fluff. Every word should earn its place.

5. .gitignore: should generated .js be gitignored or committed? (They must be committed since the workflow runtime reads them, but we need a way to tell devs "don't edit these directly")
6. DX: how does a developer know to run the build after editing .ts? Is there a watch mode?
7. Testing: how to verify the generated JS is valid for the sandbox (syntax check, no leftover imports)?

## Official Claude API Best Practices for Multi-Agent Code Generation Pipelines

Here are the concrete, documented recommendations from Anthropic for your use case:

---

### 1. **Role Prompting & System Instructions**

**Official guidance:** Yes, use role prompting in the system field. It focuses behavior without preamble overhead.

From docs:
> "Give Claude a role... Setting a role in the system prompt focuses Claude's behavior and tone for your use case. Even a single sentence makes a difference."

**For code generation agents:**
- Use system prompts like: `"You are a code generation specialist. Write production-quality code following [specific standards]."`
- Roles work best combined with **XML structuring** of the prompt (detailed below)
- **Do NOT use negative constraints in roles** — instead, use positive framing with context

### 2. **Negative Constraints vs. Positive Framing**

**Official guidance:** Positive framing is measurably more effective.

From docs:
> "Tell Claude what to do instead of what not to do"
>
> - Instead of: "Do not use markdown in your response"
> - Try: "Your response should be composed of smoothly flowing prose paragraphs."

**For evaluator agents (critical):**
- Instead of: "DO NOT hallucinate, DO NOT guess, DO NOT assume"
- Use: "Ground all findings in exact line numbers and code quotes. Before making any claim about code, read the file."

The docs explicitly note that Claude is trained to resist instructions phrased as negations, so **evidence-first patterns** (see below) are more effective.

### 3. **Structured Outputs & JSON Schema Enforcement**

**Official guidance:** Use the `client.messages.parse()` SDK method with Pydantic models for strict validation.

From docs:
```python
from pydantic import BaseModel

class GeneratedCode(BaseModel):
    code: str
    language: str
    explanation: str

response = client.messages.parse(
    model="claude-opus-4-8",
    max_tokens=2048,
    output_format=GeneratedCode,
    messages=[...]
)

generated = response.parsed_output  # Automatically validated
```

**Limitations to know:**
- Unsupported: `minimum`, `maximum`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, recursive schemas
- `enum` constraints work; use them for categorical fields
- Max 24 optional parameters total, 16 union types (`anyOf`)

**For evaluation/scoring:**
```python
class CodeReviewScore(BaseModel):
    file_path: str
    issues: list[str]  # Evidence FIRST
    risk_level: Literal["low", "medium", "high"]  # Use Literal enums
    recommendation: str
```

**Official guidance:** Use **adaptive thinking** (not extended thinking) for code generation and evaluation tasks.

From docs:
> "Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 use adaptive thinking (`thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`), where Claude dynamically decides when and how much to think. In internal evaluations, adaptive thinking reliably drives better performance than extended thinking."

**For code agents:**
```python
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-4-8",
    max_tokens=4096,
    thinking={"type": "adaptive"},
    output_config={"effort": "high"},  # Controls thinking depth
    messages=[...]
)
```

**When to use thinking for evaluators:**

This is especially valuable for evaluation tasks where Claude must reason about code quality.

**Official guidance from long-context recommendations:**

   # WRONG (query at end):
   "Here's the code: [100KB JSON]... Now generate tests"

   "[Large JSON structure]
    ...
    Now generate tests based on the structure above"

   <instruction>Generate unit tests for the following code</instruction>
   <codebase>
     <file path="datum/cli.py">
       [code here]
     </file>
     <file path="datum/core.py">
       [code here]
     </file>
   </codebase>
   <constraints>
     <model_tier>default</model_tier>
     <max_tokens>2048</max_tokens>
   </constraints>
   ```

   <instructions>
   Review the code and identify issues. 
   
   First, extract quoted lines from the code that demonstrate each issue.
   Then, explain the issue and its severity.
   </instructions>
   
   <code>

   </code>

system_prompt = """
You are a code implementation specialist. Your job is to WRITE code, not suggest changes.

When implementing functionality:
- Write complete, working implementations, not suggestions
- Use the specific patterns and models defined in the acceptance criteria
- Include all imports and dependencies
- Write production-quality code following project standards

- Read related files to understand patterns

"""
```

<investigate_before_answering>
Never speculate about code you have not opened. If asked about a specific file,

Provide grounded, hallucination-free answers based on what you actually read.

```

## 1. Role Prompting for Code Generation vs Code Evaluation

**The short answer: it depends on the task type, and generic "you are an expert" rarely helps factual accuracy.**

Result: **personas in system prompts did not improve performance** compared to a no-persona baseline. The effect of any given persona was "largely random."

- [Prompting Science Report 4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.05858) tested in-domain expert personas (e.g., physics expert for physics questions) on GPQA Diamond and MMLU-Pro across six models: **persona prompts generally did not improve accuracy relative to a no-persona baseline.**

- The [PRISM paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.18507) found a specific tradeoff: expert personas **improve alignment and tone** on generative tasks but **damage accuracy on discriminative/factual tasks**. This means role prompting helps when you want a style (code review tone, explanation style) but hurts when you need correctness (evaluation, scoring).

- One exception: [personality-guided code generation](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.00006) (MBPP, HumanEval+, APPS benchmarks) showed up to **13.8% accuracy improvement** when personality descriptions were combined with Chain-of-Thought prompting. The key: it was task-specific personality design, not generic "you are an expert."

- Anthropic's own [official best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) endorse giving Claude a role but frame it as focusing behavior and tone: "Even a single sentence makes a difference." They don't claim it improves factual accuracy.

**Actionable takeaway:** Use role prompts for **tone, scope, and behavioral constraints** (e.g., "You are a code reviewer who checks for thread safety"). Don't use them expecting factual accuracy improvements. For evaluation/scoring tasks, role prompting may actually hurt. Pair role prompts with concrete instructions, not just a title.

---

## 2. Step-by-Step Instructions vs High-Level Goals

**Research findings:**

- Anthropic's official docs state explicitly: **"Prefer general instructions over prescriptive steps.** A prompt like 'think thoroughly' often produces better reasoning than a hand-written step-by-step plan. Claude's reasoning frequently exceeds what a human would prescribe."

- Research on [agentic coding](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.19443) shows the paradigm shift: developers specify high-level objectives ("integrate an external API"), and the agent creates internal execution plans, breaking tasks into subtasks autonomously. The agent's decomposition is often better than the human's.

- However, a [2025 study on professional developer agent usage](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.14012) found that **vague prompts do not work** -- you need specificity and detail, but the detail should be about **what** you want, not **how** to do it.

- Research on [task decomposition](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.07772v1) shows decomposition is critical when tasks exceed context window limits or have complex dependencies that the model might lose track of. The structure of decomposition matters more than the content of individual steps.

- [Task capability has doubled every 4 months](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.18875) in 2024-2025, with frontier models completing 3-5 hour software engineering tasks autonomously by 2025.

**Actionable takeaway:** Decompose tasks into steps when: (a) the task has complex inter-dependencies, (b) you need to inspect intermediate outputs, (c) the task spans multiple context windows, or (d) error handling at each stage matters. Let the model plan autonomously when: (a) the task is well-defined but the approach is open-ended, (b) the model has tool access to discover context, (c) the model's reasoning capabilities exceed what you'd prescribe. In both cases, be **specific about what** you want, not **prescriptive about how**.

---

## 3. Negative Constraints ("do NOT do X")

**This is the most actionable finding of the seven. Negations are fundamentally problematic in LLMs.**

**Research findings:**

- The [Pink Elephant Problem](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.15154v1) (2024): LLMs exhibit **ironic rebound** -- after a "do not mention X" instruction, they become **more likely** to output X. Circuit tracing reveals sparse middle-layer attention heads that amplify the forbidden token under cognitive load.

- [White Bear research](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.12381) (2025) confirmed this algorithmically: attempting to suppress a concept activates it in the model's representations. This is analogous to the psychological phenomenon where "don't think about a white bear" makes you think about a white bear.

- [Negation survey](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.22395v2) (2025): Larger models handle negation better (Spearman correlation 0.867 between model size and negation accuracy), but even 70B models only reach 87-95% negation sensitivity. Negation tokens have "a limited effect on distributional representations."

- A [taxonomy of prompt defects](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.14404) identifies "ambiguous negative constraints" as a specific defect class in production LLM systems.

- Anthropic's official docs explicitly state: **"Tell Claude what to do instead of what not to do."** Example: Instead of "Do not use markdown in your response," use "Your response should be composed of smoothly flowing prose paragraphs."

**On threshold:** There's no published research giving a specific number of negations where performance collapses. But the mechanism is clear -- each negation introduces a suppression target that the model must actively work against, and under load (complex tasks, long contexts), ironic rebound increases. The practical threshold is **as few as possible**.

**Actionable takeaway:**
1. Reframe every "do NOT" as a positive instruction: "Do not use mock data" becomes "Use real production data exclusively."
2. If a negation is absolutely necessary (safety constraints), make it short, early in the prompt, and paired with a positive alternative.
3. Context/motivation improves compliance: Anthropic's docs show "NEVER use ellipses" is less effective than "Your response will be read aloud by a text-to-speech engine, so never use ellipses since the text-to-speech engine will not know how to pronounce them."
4. Audit existing prompts: count negations, convert what you can, accept that the remaining ones degrade performance proportionally.

---

## 4. Evidence Before Verdict for LLM Evaluators

**Strong evidence this works. This is one of the most well-supported patterns in the research.**

**Research findings:**

- [J1](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.10320v2) (2025): A reinforcement learning framework that trains LLM judges to reason before judging. J1-Qwen-32B achieved **76.8% accuracy on PPE Correctness** (10.3% improvement over base) and **93.6% on RewardBench**, outperforming DeepSeek-R1-671B and OpenAI o3 on several benchmarks -- with only 22K training examples.

- [G-Eval](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/llm-as-a-judge-scoring) research shows structured reasoning before scoring **improves correlation with human judgments by 10-15%** because judges explicitly evaluate each quality dimension rather than relying on surface patterns.

- The key mechanism: **by forcing the model to generate reasoning tokens before the score, it logically constrains its own final output.** It prevents hallucinating a high score that contradicts facts it just established.

- [EvalPlanner](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.15594v6) (Saha et al., 2025) takes this further: generate an evaluation plan, then execute it, then issue a verdict. The separation of plan and execution leads to more accurate judgments.

- [LLM judges agree with human reviewers ~85% of the time](https://www.braintrust.dev/articles/what-is-llm-as-a-judge) -- higher than two humans agree with each other.

- The [HALU-J framework](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/llm-as-a-judge-scoring) implements a four-stage evidence pipeline: categorize, reorder, analyze, aggregate -- all before the final verdict.

**Actionable takeaway:** Always require evidence/reasoning before verdict in evaluator prompts. In JSON schemas, put `reasoning`/`evidence`/`justification` fields **before** `score`/`verdict` fields. The 8-15% accuracy improvement is reliable and nearly free. For high-stakes evaluation, use an explicit evaluation plan (criteria list) before the reasoning step.

---

## 5. Structured JSON Output

**Research findings:**

- **Field ordering is load-bearing.** Because LLMs generate left-to-right, fields generated earlier influence fields generated later. Putting a `reasoning` field before an `answer` field improved accuracy by **8 percentage points** in aggregation tasks and **60% on GSM8k** ([Instructor blog](https://python.useinstructor.com/blog/2024/09/26/bad-schemas-could-break-your-llm-structured-outputs/), [Hannecke](https://medium.com/@michael.hannecke/beyond-json-picking-the-right-format-for-llm-pipelines-b65f15f77f7d)).

- **Constrained decoding has a cost.** Forcing JSON output via constrained decoding (token masking) can **degrade reasoning by 10-15%** ([Draft-Conditioned Constrained Decoding](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.03305)). The recommended solution is a two-step approach: let the model reason freely in natural language, then convert to structured format.

- **Specify constraints in the prompt even when using constrained decoding.** This reduces the gap between the model's natural distribution and the constrained distribution ([Think Inside the JSON](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.14905)).

- **Enum fields help.** Using enums for categorical values constrains the output space and reduces schema violations. Freeform strings in categorical fields are a common failure mode.

- **OpenAI's Structured Outputs** (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) achieved **100% schema conformance** on complex JSON evaluations, up from <40% for earlier models. The industry is converging on native structured output support.

- Anthropic recommends using their [Structured Outputs feature](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs) or tool definitions with enum fields for classification tasks.

**Actionable takeaway:**
1. Put reasoning/evidence fields before conclusion/score fields in your schema.
2. Use enums for all categorical values -- never freeform strings for categories.
3. If using constrained decoding, also describe the schema in the prompt text.
4. For reasoning-heavy tasks, consider a two-step approach: free reasoning first, then structured extraction.
5. Include `schema_version` for inter-agent schemas (your existing practice is well-supported).

---

## 6. Persona Consistency in Multi-Agent Systems

**The most surprising finding: distinct personas can significantly hurt performance.**

**Research findings:**

- [Multi-Agent Teams Hold Experts Back](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.01011v1) (2025): Multi-agent teams **underperformed their strongest individual member by 8.1% to 37.6%** across frontier ML benchmarks. On complex reasoning (Humanity's Last Exam), the gap was 37.6%. The cause: "integrative compromise" -- teams average expert and non-expert opinions instead of deferring to demonstrated expertise.

- [Biased Agents research](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.12285) (2025): Task-irrelevant persona cues caused **up to 26.2% performance degradation**. Geographic/demographic personas surfaced latent stereotype biases that disrupted task performance. This was consistent across multiple model architectures.

- [Temperature and Persona in LLM Consensus](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.11198): Personas had **minimal accuracy gains** in qualitative coding tasks while introducing variability.

- [Role Clarity research](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.02770) (2025) proposes a fix: **quantitative role-clarity supervision** -- structurally grounding role definitions rather than relying on narrative persona descriptions.

- However, heterogeneous personality teams (e.g., "stubborn" + "suggestible" agents) **outperform homogeneous teams** on complex reasoning and consensus tasks. The benefit comes from behavioral diversity, not persona flavor text.

**Actionable takeaway:** Give agents **functional roles with clear task boundaries** (critic, implementer, validator), not narrative personas ("You are a senior engineer named Alice who graduated from MIT"). Keep persona descriptions task-relevant. Avoid demographic or personality details unrelated to the task. If using multi-agent debate, ensure a mechanism for epistemic deference to the most knowledgeable agent rather than majority-vote compromise.

---

## 7. Prompt Length vs Performance

**There is a real performance cliff, and it's earlier than most people think.**

**Research findings:**

- Research found **reasoning performance degradation at around 3,000 tokens** -- well below the technical context window limits of modern LLMs ([Grit Daily](https://gritdaily.com/impact-prompt-length-llm-performance/)).

- For moderately complex tasks, the optimal prompt length is **150-300 words** (~200-400 tokens). Performance begins degrading past **500 words** (~650 tokens) ([MLOps Community](https://mlops.community/blog/the-impact-of-prompt-bloat-on-llm-output-quality)).

- The [Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.10276v1) phenomenon: accuracy drops **>30%** for information positioned in the middle of the context. This U-shaped retrieval pattern replicated across six model families (GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4, Claude 1.3, LongChat-13B, MPT-30B, Cohere Command).

- Every extra 500 tokens increases response latency by ~25ms and reduces available space for conversation history.

- Anthropic's official guidance for long contexts: **put long documents at the top, queries at the bottom.** "Queries at the end can improve response quality by up to 30% in tests, especially with complex, multi-document inputs."

- Chain-of-thought prompting **does not mitigate** the degradation from excessive input length.

**Actionable takeaway:**
1. System prompts should be as concise as possible. Every rule you add has a cost.
2. For long system prompts (like CLAUDE.md files), front-load the most critical rules and put reference material at the end.
3. Put long documents/context at the top, instructions/queries at the bottom.
4. Periodically audit system prompts for redundant or obsolete rules -- each one is paying a tax on every response.
5. Consider your CLAUDE.md: if it exceeds ~3,000 tokens of system prompt, the rules in the middle are getting the weakest attention.

---

1	# Multi-Agent TDD Pipeline: Prompt Engineering Research & Recommendations
2	
3	## Research Synthesis
4	
5	### Cross-Cutting Findings
6	
7	Before diving into per-agent recommendations, here are the research-backed principles that apply across all 8 agents:
8	
9	#### 1. Role Framing
10	
11	**Finding:** Anthropic's model migration guide confirms 4.6+ models follow instructions far more literally. "CRITICAL: YOU MUST" language overtriggers. Academic research reinforces this: a peer-reviewed EMNLP 2024 study (Zheng et al., arXiv:2311.10054) tested 162 role personas across 4 LLM families on 2,410 factual questions and found **personas in system prompts did not improve factual performance** vs a no-persona baseline. The PRISM paper (arXiv:2603.18507) found a specific tradeoff: expert personas **improve alignment and tone** on generative tasks but **damage accuracy on discriminative/evaluation tasks**. One exception: personality-guided code generation (arXiv:2411.00006) showed up to 13.8% accuracy improvement when task-specific personality was combined with CoT -- but generic "you are an expert" had no effect.
12	
13	**Implication for this pipeline:** Role statements for code-writing agents (RED, GREEN, REFACTOR) should be brief and functional -- "RED TDD agent" not "You are an expert senior software engineer." For evaluator agents (REFLECT, SKEPTIC), role framing should focus on **behavioral constraints** ("Read-only evaluator") not expertise claims, since the PRISM research shows expert personas hurt discriminative accuracy.
14	
15	#### 2. Task Decomposition: Steps vs Goals
16	
17	**Finding:** Anthropic's docs state: "Prefer general instructions over prescriptive steps. A prompt like 'think thoroughly' often produces better reasoning than a hand-written step-by-step plan." The migration guide notes "prompts written for prior models are often too prescriptive and reduce output quality." Research on agentic coding (arXiv:2505.19443) confirms: agents create better internal execution plans when given high-level objectives than when micromanaged. However, a 2025 study on professional developer agent usage (arXiv:2512.14012) found **vague prompts don't work** -- you need specificity about **what** you want, not **how** to do it.
18	
19	**Implication:** RED, GREEN, and REFACTOR agents should get clear goals + constraints, not step-by-step procedures. GIT COMMIT should keep numbered steps (it's a mechanical procedure). Evaluators should get explicit criteria + format requirements.
20	
21	#### 3. Negative Constraints: The "Don't" Problem
22	
23	**Finding:** This is the most well-supported finding in the research. The Pink Elephant Problem (arXiv:2404.15154, 2024) demonstrates LLMs exhibit **ironic rebound** -- after "do not mention X," they become MORE likely to output X. Circuit tracing reveals sparse middle-layer attention heads that amplify the forbidden token under cognitive load. White Bear research (arXiv:2511.12381, 2025) confirmed this algorithmically. A negation survey (arXiv:2503.22395, 2025) found even 70B models only reach 87-95% negation sensitivity. Anthropic's own docs explicitly state: "Tell Claude what to do instead of what not to do." Adding context/motivation for WHY a constraint exists improves compliance significantly.
24	
25	**Implication:** The current RED prompt has 6 negative rules -- this is in the danger zone. Reframe most "do NOT" as positive instructions. Keep negative framing only for hard safety boundaries (git commands, file ownership) where there's no positive equivalent. Adding a reason for each constraint ("NEVER use NotImplementedError -- conftest will xfail it") is already a good practice that should be extended.
26	
27	#### 4. Evidence-First Patterns for Evaluators
28	
29	**Finding:** The strongest finding in the entire research. J1 (arXiv:2505.10320, 2025) trained LLM judges to reason before judging, achieving 76.8% accuracy on PPE Correctness (10.3% improvement over base). G-Eval research shows structured reasoning before scoring **improves correlation with human judgments by 10-15%**. The mechanism is clear: by forcing the model to generate reasoning tokens before the score, it logically constrains its own output and prevents hallucinating a high score that contradicts facts it just established. Additionally, field ordering research (Instructor blog, arXiv) demonstrates **8 percentage point accuracy improvement** by putting reasoning fields before answer fields in JSON schemas.
30	
31	The SKEPTIC_SCHEMA currently has `bugs_found` before `verdict` (correct). REFLECT_SCHEMA has `score` before `reasoning` (inverted -- the model picks a number then rationalizes it).
32	
33	**Implication:** All evaluator schemas must enforce evidence-before-verdict field ordering. REFLECT schema needs `reasoning` -> `gaps` -> `score`. This single change is expected to be the highest-impact improvement in the entire plan.
34	
35	#### 5. Chain-of-Thought vs Direct Output
36	
37	**Finding:** For code generation (RED, GREEN, REFACTOR), direct output is preferred -- the model should write code, not explain its reasoning in prose. For evaluation (REFLECT, SKEPTIC, REFACTOR_CHECK), chain-of-thought improves quality. Anthropic recommends adaptive thinking for complex reasoning; at the API level this maps to `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`, but at the prompt level for Claude Code `agent()` calls, it means we should ask evaluators to show their work in the output schema.
38	
39	**Implication:** Code-writing agents: no "think step by step" -- just write code. Evaluators: require reasoning/evidence before scores.
40	
41	#### 6. Structured Output Alignment
42	
43	**Finding:** Anthropic's docs emphasize: (a) use enums for categorical values, (b) field ordering matters, (c) simpler schemas produce more reliable output. Research adds two important nuances: (1) Constrained JSON decoding can **degrade reasoning by 10-15%** (arXiv:2603.03305) because token masking conflicts with the model's natural distribution. The recommended solution: let the model reason freely, then extract structure. (2) Even when using constrained decoding, **specifying constraints in the prompt text** (not just the schema) reduces the gap (arXiv:2502.14905). The current SKEPTIC_SCHEMA has `severity` as a free-form string -- should be an enum.
44	
45	**Implication:** Add enums where appropriate. Simplify schemas. Make field ordering deliberate. The Claude Code `agent()` function uses schema enforcement, so also describe expected output shape in the prompt text (belt and suspenders).
46	
47	#### 7. Multi-Agent Persona Design: Functional Roles, Not Narrative Personas
48	
49	**Finding:** This was the most surprising research result. "Multi-Agent Teams Hold Experts Back" (arXiv:2602.01011, 2025) found multi-agent teams **underperformed their strongest individual member by 8.1% to 37.6%** on frontier ML benchmarks due to "integrative compromise" -- averaging expert and non-expert opinions. Biased Agents research (arXiv:2602.12285, 2025) found task-irrelevant persona cues caused **up to 26.2% performance degradation**. Role Clarity research (arXiv:2604.02770, 2025) proposes the fix: **quantitative role-clarity supervision** -- structurally grounding role definitions rather than narrative persona descriptions.
50	
51	**Implication:** The current pipeline's functional role design (RED writes tests, GREEN writes code, SKEPTIC reviews) is correct. Do NOT add narrative persona flavor ("You are a meticulous senior engineer who takes pride in..."). Keep role descriptions to functional task boundaries with clear input/output contracts.
52	
53	#### 8. Prompt Length: The 3,000-Token Cliff
54	
55	**Finding:** Research found reasoning performance degradation at around 3,000 tokens of prompt input. For moderately complex tasks, optimal prompt length is 150-300 words (~200-400 tokens), with degradation past 500 words. The Lost in the Middle phenomenon (arXiv:2510.10276) shows accuracy drops >30% for information positioned in the middle of long contexts. Anthropic's guidance: "Put long documents at the top, queries at the bottom."
56	
57	**Implication:** The current prompts are well under the 3,000-token cliff (most are 60-280 tokens). The proposed rewrites add tokens but stay well within safe bounds. However, the JSON task packets appended to prompts can push total input higher -- the most critical instructions should appear at the START of the prompt (before the packet), not after it.
58	
59	#### 9. Context Window Efficiency
60	
61	**Finding:** The agent design docs recommend keeping fixed context small and loading detail on demand. The current prompts embed entire JSON task packets inline in the prompt string. Better: reference the packet file path and let the agent read it, OR structure the packet so the most critical fields come first.
62	
63	**Implication:** The current approach of embedding the full packet is acceptable for smaller packets but the GREEN packet (which includes `preflight`, `impl_stubs`, `existing_api`) can be large. The prompt should front-load the critical information (what to do, what files to write) and put supplementary context (existing_api shape) last.
64	
65	---
66	
67	## Per-Agent Analysis & Recommendations
68	
69	---
70	
71	### 1. RED TDD Agent (model: sonnet)
72
